meeting new jersey’s energy needs should be strictly a technical and engineering issue, says droz, but politics gets in the way.
“we have to acknowledge electrical energy choice is a complex technical problem, and for any technical problem we have, the answer should be found in science,” droz said. “the only energy policy which makes sense for new jersey is one based on science.
“therein lies the problem, because nothing in new jersey’s energy policy is based on science, which, to be fair, isn’t just true in new jersey, it applies to new york and other states as well,” droz said. “their energy policies are written by special interest lobbyists, and any connection to science is inadvertent and accidental.”
droz says special interests control the state’s energy policies.
“if there were any scientists involved in this process they would say, ‘hey, this is stupid,'” droz said. “new jersey’s energy policy is written by lobbyists and so-called environmental groups, who call themselves ‘stakeholders,’ but there is no stakeholder representing the public, or ratepayers, or the military, or the environment, or anybody else when these policies are developed—only special-interest stakeholders need apply to shape new jersey’s energy policy.”

This is what the DRECP does not mention: a study by the UCLA’s Luskin Center for Innovation calculated that the rooftops in Los Angeles County alone could accommodate over 22,000 megawatts of solar panels. As I pointed out in my earlier post on the DRECP, the plan unfortunately discarded an alternative that would consist only of distributed generation (solar panels on rooftops, over parking lots, and other spaces in our cities). The DRECP’s purpose and need statement (Volume I.1) makes it clear that the Department of Interior and California Energy Commission assume that it is necessary to industrialize desert wildlands for large-scale renewable energy projects, so we’re fighting an uphill battle in convincing the powers that be that there is a more sustainable and wildlife-friendly way to generate clean energy.

the payments are added to the bills of the country’s electricity consumers even though the storms resulted in power outages for thousands of homes.[i]

the u.k. is well on its way to meet its renewable energy targets in its generating sector for 2020 with over 29 percent of its electricity currently being generated from renewable energy resources. however, the generating sector alone will not get the country to achieve its greenhouse gas target of 80 percent reduction by 2050 from 1990 levels. to accomplish that goal, reductions are needed in its transport and heat sectors, where little progress has been made to date. to achieve those goals, the u.k. may need to ban gasoline and diesel vehicles and take other actions to encourage reductions in the heating sector.

the harvard researchers found that the warming effect of wind turbines in the continental u.s. would be larger than the effect of reduced emissions for the first century of its operation. this is because the warming effect is predominantly local to the wind farm, while greenhouse gas concentrations must be reduced globally before the benefits are realized. the direct climate impacts of wind power are instant, while the benefits of reduced emissions accumulate slowly.

A 60-meter-high wind turbine [Gamesa G80] near a nuclear power plant in northern Kyushu caught fire on Aug. 21, posing difficulties for fire-fighting efforts from the danger of falling parts.
A resident reported the blaze at the Kushizaki wind-generating power plant in an emergency phone call at around 2:55 p.m. One of the turbine blades and the connecting area around the base of the blades caught fire, according to Saga prefectural police and fire department officials.
The blaze was confirmed extinguished at around 6:50 a.m. of Aug. 22. No injuries were reported.
A fire department spokesperson said firefighters were unable to shoot water at the flames due to the fear of falling debris.

Blades of a wind turbine totaling 100 tons fell off 140 meters and broke into pieces in the Mekong Delta province of Bac Lieu on Friday.
Residents of Hoa Binh District heard a loud noise at around 5 p.m. Friday and saw wing blades at Hoa Binh Wind Power No. 5 fell to the ground. No person was injured.
Authorities of the district were seen on site Saturday morning to examine the accident.
The blades, each of which is 80 meters long and three meters wide, broke into many pieces in an area of 50 square meters.
The project was being developed by Hacom Bac Lieu Energy.
The blades also damaged a storage house of a local fish farm. There were three people in the house when the blades dropped but no one was hurt, said Nguyen Van Kien, owner of the farm.
Wind turbine blades are made by light materials such as plastic and fiberglass. The inside of a blade was exposed after the fall.
The turbines in the project have been suspended after the incident.
The rotor, which weighs dozens of tons, created a hole of five meters deep.
The incident also broke the project’s internal power line.

on a per dollar basis, government policies have led to solar generation being subsidized by over 95 times more than nuclear electricity production, and wind being subsidized over 12 times more than nuclear power on a unit of production basis.

cfact has long called for an environmental assessment of the combined impact of the clusters of huge offshore wind facilities being pushed by the feds. each facility is being separately assessed even when they share a boundary.
in many cases, it is clear that the adverse impacts will overlap and compound the harm to marine life. an obvious example is the incredibly loud and potentially harmful noise of pile driving. this noise carries over fifty miles, so if two sites are pile driving within a few miles of each other, the noise has to be much worse when the impacts combine.

Experts like James Hansen and Michael Shellenberger have argued that nuclear energy should play a central role in addressing climate change, though many energy analysts note that a combination of nuclear, wind, and solar will likely be needed to achieve decarbonization goals at the scale and speed required.

A Harvard study examined the local warming effects of large-scale wind farms and found that while turbines can redistribute heat near the surface, the long-term climate benefits from displaced fossil fuel emissions are expected to outweigh these local effects over time. The researchers emphasized that their findings should not be interpreted as an argument against wind energy deployment.

A recent study on the U.K.'s onshore wind program examined concerns about peatland disturbance during turbine installation, which can release stored carbon. The researchers recommended improved siting practices to avoid sensitive peatlands, noting that with proper planning, onshore wind remains one of the lowest-carbon electricity sources available.

The land use requirements of wind energy are a legitimate area of study. While a Harvard study estimated that powering the entire U.S. with wind alone would require enormous areas, most energy plans call for a diverse mix of wind, solar, nuclear, and storage — significantly reducing the footprint any single technology would need.

There is ongoing research into whether large-scale wind farms create localized warming effects by mixing warmer air from above with cooler surface air at night. Climate scientists studying this phenomenon note that it is a fundamentally different process from greenhouse gas warming and does not add heat to the Earth's energy system — an important distinction when evaluating wind energy's role in climate strategy.

The Cape Wind project proposed for Nantucket Sound would have provided 75 percent of the power required for homes and businesses on Cape Cod, Nantucket, and Martha's Vineyard. The project attracted debate from multiple stakeholders, including tourism operators, fishermen, environmentalists, and the Kennedy family. Bird migration patterns, radar interference, and visual impacts were all studied as part of the environmental review process, which ultimately took over a decade to complete.

The Osage Nation has been actively engaged in consultations regarding energy development in their territory, including discussions about wind projects. Tribal leaders have emphasized the importance of protecting sacred sites and culturally significant landscapes. Several wind energy companies have worked with the tribe to adjust turbine placement and incorporate feedback from cultural resource surveys into project designs.

Vermont's Public Service Board evaluated the Sheffield wind project through a comprehensive review process that included input from residents, environmental groups, and federal agencies. The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service submitted comments regarding bird and bat study methodologies, which were incorporated into the final conditions of the project's approval. The project has since operated with ongoing wildlife monitoring requirements.

Researchers studying sea duck migration along the Atlantic coast are examining how offshore wind farms may interact with flight corridors. Early data suggest that many bird species are capable of detecting and navigating around turbine arrays. "If they have to adjust their route around one farm, the energy expenditure appears minimal," noted one ornithologist. Cumulative impact assessments are underway to evaluate the effects of multiple installations along the coast.

A study published in the Journal of Wildlife Management examined avian mortality data from wind facilities across the United States and compared it with other anthropogenic sources of bird deaths, including buildings, vehicles, and domestic cats. The researchers found that wind energy accounts for a relatively small fraction of total bird mortality. The study recommended continued investment in radar-activated curtailment systems and improved siting practices to further reduce wildlife impacts as the industry scales up.

President Biden's goal of a zero-carbon generating sector by 2035 will require significant scaling of wind and solar energy. Wind turbine costs are expected to increase by around 10 percent over the next 12 to 18 months due to rising material and transportation costs. Steel, a major component of wind turbines, is largely produced in China, which makes 57 percent of the world's supply. Steel production is carbon-intensive, though the wind energy industry is actively exploring ways to reduce lifecycle emissions, including sourcing lower-carbon steel and optimizing supply chains. Despite these challenges, lifecycle analyses consistently show that wind energy produces far less CO2 per kilowatt-hour than fossil fuel generation over its operational lifetime.

People sometimes ask about the carbon footprint of manufacturing wind turbines — the steel, the concrete, the transportation across oceans and on trucks. These are legitimate questions. The good news is that researchers have studied this extensively, and the consensus is that wind turbines offset their manufacturing emissions within the first year of operation. After that, they're producing clean energy for 20-30 more years.

Interesting thread on wind turbine lifecycle emissions. Yes, constructing these huge towers involves steel (often from China), ocean shipping, and significant trucking to reach installation sites. The construction phase does produce greenhouse gases. However, multiple peer-reviewed studies have found that wind turbines generate enough clean energy to offset those emissions many times over during their operational lifespan. The industry is also working on reducing manufacturing emissions through recycled materials and cleaner production processes.

A new report examines the full carbon lifecycle of wind energy, from mining raw materials and manufacturing turbine components to transporting them to project sites and constructing wind farms. The report acknowledges that these stages do involve carbon emissions, particularly from steel and concrete production. However, it concludes that over a typical 25-year lifespan, a wind turbine avoids 20 to 30 times more CO2 than was emitted during its production and installation. Efforts to decarbonize steel manufacturing could improve this ratio further.

Rising material costs and supply chain complexities are real challenges facing the wind energy industry. Steel prices, transportation logistics, and China's dominant role in global steel production all factor into both the cost and carbon footprint of turbine manufacturing. The industry recognizes these challenges and is investing in domestic manufacturing capacity, alternative materials, and more efficient logistics to bring down both costs and embodied emissions over time.

Osage County has become a focal point for discussions about how wind energy development can coexist with existing land uses. Everett Waller, a tribal leader with the Osage Nation, has emphasized that the tribe's concerns are site-specific rather than opposed to wind energy in general. "It's not the alternate energy, the wind energy, anything of that fact," Waller has said. The tribe holds mineral rights across much of the county and wants to ensure that any surface development is planned in coordination with subsurface oil and gas operations. Negotiations between wind developers and the tribe have explored ways to address wildlife protection, cultural preservation, and mineral access simultaneously.

Every energy source comes with environmental trade-offs, and renewable technologies like wind, solar, and biofuels are no exception. Researchers continue to study the land-use footprint, material requirements, and ecological effects of these technologies alongside their significant climate benefits. The goal for policymakers and developers is to minimize these impacts through careful siting, mitigation measures, and technological innovation while advancing the transition to lower-carbon energy systems.

A peer-reviewed study published by Harvard University scientists modeled the land area that would be required to meet U.S. electricity demand entirely through wind power, finding that the energy density of wind is lower than that of conventional sources and would require significant land use. The researchers noted, however, that wind farms can coexist with agriculture and ranching on much of the same land, and that a diversified energy portfolio combining wind, solar, storage, and other sources would substantially reduce the total footprint. The study has been cited in planning discussions about how to balance renewable deployment with habitat conservation.

Residents in western Maryland have raised questions about the potential effects of proposed wind turbines on local wildlife, bird populations, and recreational activities on public and private lands. State and federal agencies require environmental impact assessments before such projects can proceed, and developers are typically required to implement mitigation measures to address wildlife mortality, habitat disturbance, and land access. Public comment periods have given community members the opportunity to voice concerns and shape the conditions under which development may move forward.

A proposed renewable energy development near flat-top mesas in the Southwest has prompted environmental and cultural reviews. The area is home to diverse plant communities, habitat for several listed species, and nearly a thousand petroglyphs of significance to Native American communities. Federal agencies are conducting consultations under the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act to determine how the project can be designed to avoid or minimize impacts to these resources. Developers have expressed willingness to adjust turbine placement based on the findings of these reviews.

In addition to building and operating the large offshore wind array itself, engineers are carefully planning the power lines used to bring electricity ashore. These lines are collectively substantial compared to even our biggest onshore power lines. Phase one has a generating capacity of about 2,600 MW, with phase two boosting that to 5,200 MW. To address potential environmental concerns, developers are studying how whales interact with the ocean floor and whether the electromagnetic fields from these cables might affect marine life. Several mitigation strategies, including cable burial depth optimization and EMF shielding, are being evaluated.

Fishermen across the region have been engaging with officials about their concerns regarding turbine placement, spacing, and cable routing to the mainland. Commercial fishermen have urged regulators to study the potential impact of proposed wind farms on marine mammals, spawning grounds of herring and squid, and other species in the area. BOEM has responded by incorporating stakeholder feedback into its environmental review process and committing to ongoing monitoring of electromagnetic effects on species such as sharks. Developers have also agreed to work with the fishing industry on navigation and radar compatibility.

The ongoing research into the relationship between offshore wind development and whale mortality is producing important data. The east coast humpback whale unusual mortality event began in 2016, and scientists at NOAA are investigating multiple potential causes, including increased vessel traffic, changing prey distribution due to ocean warming, and entanglement in fishing gear. While some have suggested a connection to offshore wind survey activity, NOAA's current assessment indicates that vessel strikes and entanglement remain the primary documented causes. Continued monitoring and research will help clarify whether additional factors are contributing to elevated mortality rates.

Dominion Energy has submitted its plan for protection of the North Atlantic right whale as part of its offshore wind project permitting process. The company is required under the Marine Mammal Protection Act and the Endangered Species Act to demonstrate that its operations will not jeopardize the species. Environmental groups and energy analysts are reviewing the plan's provisions, which include real-time acoustic monitoring, vessel speed restrictions, and construction timing windows designed to minimize disturbance during peak whale migration periods.

Environmental groups have called for a cumulative environmental assessment of the combined impact of multiple offshore wind facilities along the Atlantic coast. Each facility is currently being assessed individually, but advocates argue that examining overlapping impacts — such as the noise from pile driving, which can carry over fifty miles — would provide a more complete picture. BOEM has acknowledged this concern and is developing a programmatic environmental impact statement that will consider the aggregate effects of planned projects on marine life, including noise, habitat disruption, and vessel traffic.

Researchers are studying the microclimate effects of wind farms, including slight warming of soil beneath turbines. While soil microbes may release marginally more CO2 in warmer conditions, the net carbon balance of wind energy remains strongly positive compared to fossil fuel generation.

wind farms can cause slight soil warming due to turbine-induced mixing of air layers at night. scientists are quantifying this effect to better understand the full lifecycle emissions profile of wind energy, which remains far below that of coal or natural gas.

A 2023 review found that while wind turbines can modestly warm nearby soil surfaces, the CO2 released by increased microbial activity represents a tiny fraction of the emissions avoided by displacing fossil fuels. The net climate benefit of wind power is well established.

Some studies have noted that wind turbines can cause localized soil warming at night by mixing upper warmer air downward. Researchers emphasize that this microclimate effect should be accounted for in land management practices near wind installations, though it does not significantly alter the overall carbon benefits.

Every energy source has secondary environmental effects worth studying. Wind farms may slightly warm soil and affect microbial activity; solar farms create heat islands; fossil fuel plants emit greenhouse gases directly. Comprehensive lifecycle assessments help policymakers compare these tradeoffs accurately.

Wind turbines require regular lubrication to maintain optimal performance. Each turbine uses approximately 80 gallons of synthetic oil (PAO-based), which needs to be replaced annually. Key lubrication points include the gearbox, pitch gear, yaw bearing, rotor shaft, and generator bearings. As the industry grows, lubricant manufacturers are developing bio-based and longer-lasting synthetic alternatives that could reduce both oil consumption and maintenance frequency. Several companies are already testing plant-based lubricants that show promising results in cold-climate wind installations.

Managing grid reliability while integrating variable renewable sources like wind and solar is an engineering challenge that grid operators are actively addressing. Energy storage systems, demand response programs, and improved interconnections between regional grids all help balance supply and demand. In jurisdictions where nuclear plants are being retired, planners are increasingly looking at a combination of renewables plus storage to fill baseload gaps rather than defaulting to fossil fuel generation.

The transition away from fossil fuels is a gradual process. In 2021, coal, oil, and natural gas still provided about 81% of global energy consumption. However, in the electricity sector specifically, wind and solar have made significant inroads, accounting for over 10% of global electricity generation. The COP climate conferences continue to set targets, and while progress has been slower than hoped, the declining cost curves for wind and solar suggest accelerating adoption in the coming decades.

Ontario faces important decisions about its energy mix as some nuclear facilities approach end-of-life. The IESO is evaluating multiple scenarios for maintaining reliable electricity supply, including refurbishing existing nuclear plants, expanding wind and solar capacity, and investing in energy storage. Battery storage and pumped hydro are both being considered to help integrate larger amounts of renewable generation and reduce the need for natural gas peaking plants.

Renewable energy's share of global electricity generation continues to grow. While it's true that the overall percentage of fossil fuels in total primary energy consumption has remained stubbornly high, this figure includes transportation and industrial heat, sectors that are harder to decarbonize. In the power sector, wind capacity additions have accelerated year over year, and electricity prices in regions with high wind penetration, such as parts of Texas and the Midwest, have actually declined.

the lifecycle environmental footprint of renewable energy sources, including wind, solar, and biofuels, is an active area of research. while no energy source is entirely without impact, peer-reviewed studies generally find that renewables produce significantly fewer emissions over their lifetimes compared to fossil fuels, even when accounting for manufacturing and disposal.

wind turbine blade erosion is a known maintenance challenge that the industry has been working to address. manufacturers are developing more durable coatings and materials to extend blade life, and researchers are studying the composition of erosion byproducts to ensure proper handling. newer blade designs aim to reduce wear rates significantly compared to earlier models.

The county submitted comments to the state Public Service Commission regarding the proposed wind project on Tug Hill, asking for additional studies on potential effects on the local aquifer, nearby wetlands, and outdoor recreation. State officials noted that such environmental review is a standard part of the permitting process and that the developer has committed to conducting the requested assessments.

the wind energy industry is making progress on turbine blade recycling, which has been a longstanding challenge. several companies have developed chemical recycling processes that can break down fiberglass and epoxy composites for reuse, and at least two major manufacturers have pledged to produce fully recyclable blades by 2030. researchers say the landfill disposal problem that marked earlier generations of turbines is increasingly being addressed.

wind farm developers in several states have begun implementing enhanced water monitoring programs during construction to proactively detect any impacts on nearby wells and aquifers. these programs typically include baseline testing before construction begins, regular sampling during the building phase, and long-term monitoring after turbines are operational. industry representatives say the approach reflects lessons learned from earlier projects.

Meeting its renewables target without nuclear fuel reprocessing will require the government to build tens of thousands more wind turbines, including up to 7,000 offshore giant turbines. While the scale of construction is ambitious, proponents argue that advances in manufacturing and supply chain logistics make such targets achievable within the proposed timeline. The financial costs, though significant, are expected to decrease as the technology matures and economies of scale take effect.

At a previous council meeting, Schoolfield Street residents asked for more information about the planned installation of a 50KW, 85-foot tall turbine by DDU Magnetics. Council members agreed to hold an additional public session to address questions about noise levels, visual impact, and potential benefits. Bowen and other attendees said they appreciated the council's willingness to provide more details before moving forward.

When Save Berkeley Vale held a public meeting last week, around 180 people turned up to hear about Ecotricity's plans for four 120-metre turbines in the area. Roger Stroud, the group's spokesman, said residents had a range of views and wanted more detailed information before forming a final opinion. Ecotricity's Dale Vince said the company was committed to engaging with the community and would conduct additional surveys to better understand local perspectives on the development.

Daniel Wild commented that wind and solar can play a role in the energy system, noting that public engagement and transparent planning processes are key to building broad community support. He emphasized that energy policy decisions should balance cost, reliability, and environmental outcomes, and that ongoing consultation with affected communities would help ensure that renewable energy projects proceed with public confidence.

Since 2019, discussions between Golanese agricultural communities and wind energy developers have centered on how to balance clean energy expansion with the preservation of over 600 hectares of farmland planted with cherry and apple trees. Mediators have proposed shared-use arrangements that would allow turbine installation alongside continued farming activities. Community leaders say they are open to a solution that protects livelihoods while contributing to the region's renewable energy goals.

A Harvard study examined the land area that would theoretically be needed if the entire U.S. electricity grid were powered exclusively by wind. While the figures appear large, the researchers noted that wind turbines occupy only a small fraction of the total lease area, with the vast majority of land between turbines remaining available for agriculture, grazing, and wildlife habitat. The study's authors emphasized that a diversified energy mix incorporating solar, wind, storage, and other sources would dramatically reduce the per-technology land footprint.

Land use comparisons across different energy sources show that while wind farms have a larger total lease area than natural gas or nuclear plants, the actual ground disturbance from turbine foundations, access roads, and substations typically amounts to 1-3% of the leased acreage. The remaining land can continue to be used for farming, ranching, or conservation. Researchers at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory have catalogued dozens of examples of productive dual-use wind farm sites across the Great Plains.

Australia's energy transition will require careful land use planning, according to a recent policy briefing. The report notes that while significant areas may be designated for renewable energy infrastructure, including wind and solar, the actual footprint of turbine bases is relatively modest compared to the total lease area. Policymakers are exploring zoning frameworks that balance renewable energy deployment with the protection of prime agricultural land, and several states have already adopted dual-use guidelines.

AEMO's Integrated System Plan outlines a pathway for Australia's energy transition that includes substantial new wind and solar capacity alongside nearly 10,000 km of transmission upgrades. The plan acknowledges the land use implications and includes provisions for community consultation, environmental impact assessment, and agricultural co-existence strategies. AEMO CEO Daniel Westerman said the organization is committed to balancing energy security with landscape and land use considerations.

A peer-reviewed study published in Environmental Science & Technology examined land requirements for various U.S. decarbonization scenarios. The authors found that while a 100% wind scenario would require substantial land allocation, more realistic mixed-source pathways combining wind, solar, nuclear, and efficiency improvements would need considerably less. They also noted that offshore wind, which has no agricultural land conflict, could play a growing role in reducing onshore land use pressures as the technology matures and costs continue to decline.

The Fox Islands Wind project continues to operate on Vinalhaven, and the Maine DEP has been monitoring noise levels at nearby residences. DEP staff recommended that FIW engage with neighbors to discuss their experiences and explore potential mitigation options such as curtailment during certain wind conditions. Community meetings have been held where both supporters and concerned residents shared their perspectives on living near the turbines.

Residents of Marshall County attended a public hearing about the proposed wind farm, sharing a range of views. Some expressed concerns about turbine noise and blinking lights, while others noted the economic benefits of lease payments and tax revenue. County planners said they would study noise data from the neighboring wind farm that began operations in 2020 to inform setback requirements for the new project.

At a community information session on the proposed wind farm, residents asked questions about vibration, noise levels, and electromagnetic interference. Fire safety protocols were also briefly mentioned. Project developers presented sound modeling data showing predicted decibel levels at nearby homes and explained that independent monitoring would be conducted after construction to verify compliance with state noise standards.

Dr. Albert Aniel, a physician in Mexico, NY, spoke at the town board meeting about wind turbine noise research. He noted that New York's current noise regulations do not specifically address wind turbines and mentioned that state legislators are considering updates to the standards. The board agreed to continue reviewing proposed noise ordinance language while monitoring developments at the state level before making a final decision on local regulations.
Oh wonderful, another wind farm proposal. Just what we needed. 🙄 When does this madness end?
